title: Mint Sauce
subtitle: Fresh mint, vinegar, and sugar — the lamb companion
excerpt: The classic British condiment for roast lamb: fresh mint leaves finely chopped with a pinch of sugar, then dissolved in boiling water and sharpened with malt vinegar. Serves with everything from a roast leg to a chop.

recipe.sourceNotes: Mint sauce is one of the oldest documented British condiments, appearing in recipe collections from the seventeenth century as a standard companion to lamb. The combination reflects the British tradition of serving meat with an acidic accompaniment that cuts through the fat. Mint was widely grown in English kitchen gardens from Roman times onwards, and the combination with malt vinegar is distinctly British: French cooks who discovered the pairing were reportedly appalled, though the version they later adapted (in the form of a mint jelly or mint chutney) became similarly entrenched. The important technique is to dissolve the sugar in a little boiling water before adding the vinegar: this draws out the flavour from the mint and softens the sharp edge of the acid.

content.text: Use fresh mint and chop it finely so the leaves release their aromatic oils. The boiling water dissolves the sugar and wilts the mint slightly, tempering the raw edge. Malt vinegar is the traditional choice; white wine vinegar gives a cleaner result if preferred. Make it at least 30 minutes before serving so the flavours have time to meld.
Put the chopped mint and sugar in a small bowl or jug. Pour 2 tablespoons of just-boiled water over and stir until the sugar dissolves. Leave for 5 minutes.

Add the vinegar and a pinch of salt. Stir, taste, and adjust: add more sugar if too sharp, more vinegar if too mild. Set aside for at least 30 minutes before serving so the flavours develop. Serve at room temperature.
